R06-B-01: Few environmental gestures are as photogenic as planting a tree. A minister kneels with a spade, a schoolchild pats soil around a sapling, and a campaign announces that so many million trees have gone into the ground this season. The appeal is easy to understand. A tree is a visible, countable object, and counting is what campaigns need: a target can be set, met and reported. Yet the habit of measuring forest recovery by the number of saplings planted has quietly confused an input with an outcome, and the confusion has consequences for the land it is meant to help. The first problem is survival. A sapling planted in the wrong season, in compacted soil or without anyone to water it through its first dry months often dies within a year or two, and a campaign that counts plantings rather than living trees will never record the loss. The second problem is choice. Large drives tend to favour a few fast-growing species that nurseries can raise cheaply and in bulk, and the result, where the saplings do survive, may be closer to a plantation than a forest: rows of a single kind of tree, offering little to the insects, birds and fungi that a mixed woodland supports. In some places such planting has even been carried out on grasslands that were never forested at all, replacing one valuable habitat with a poor imitation of another. An alternative, less dramatic and much harder to photograph, is to let forests come back on their own. On land where old roots, nearby seed-bearing trees and a living soil remain, simply protecting an area from grazing, fire and clearing can allow a varied forest to regenerate, often more cheaply than planting and with species suited to the site because they arrived there by themselves. Regeneration of this kind is slow at first, and for some years the land looks like scrub, which is one reason it is undervalued: it does not look like progress. None of this means that planting is always a mistake. Where soils are badly degraded, where no seed sources survive nearby, or where a particular species must be reintroduced, careful planting may be the only way to begin. The objection is not to the spade but to the scoreboard. A campaign that measured success by the area of land that becomes, and remains, a functioning forest after ten or twenty years would sometimes plant and sometimes refrain, and it would be judged by what grew rather than by what was put into the ground.
R06-B-02: Conservation has always had favourites. Appeals for money are illustrated with tigers, pandas, whales and elephants, animals with large eyes, recognisable faces and a reputation for grandeur, and rarely with a beetle, a freshwater mussel or a lichen. Critics have long complained that this distorts priorities. If donors give to what they find beautiful, the argument runs, then most of the living world, which is small, drab or simply invisible, will be neglected, and the species most in need of help will be the least likely to receive it. The objection is not merely aesthetic. Insects, fungi and the small organisms of soil and water do much of the work that keeps ecosystems running, yet they attract only a tiny share of public concern. The complaint has force, but it is weaker than it first appears, because a charismatic animal rarely receives protection on its own. A large predator needs a large area, and the forest or grassland that is protected for its sake also shelters thousands of less appealing species that no donor would have paid to save directly. In this sense the famous animal works as a kind of advertisement for an entire landscape. The money is raised in the name of one face, but it is spent, at least in part, on soil, water and cover that serve everything living there. The defence holds only up to a point, however. Some of the most threatened organisms live in habitats that no charismatic animal shares: a single cave, a spring, a patch of chalk grassland, the gravel bed of one river. Protecting a tiger reserve will do nothing for them. Moreover, money given in the name of a famous animal is sometimes spent on that animal directly, on breeding programmes, tracking collars or patrols against poachers, rather than on the wider habitat, and in such cases the advertising argument does not apply at all. A donor who pays for a radio collar has helped one tiger, and perhaps the scientists who follow it, but not the river below the reserve. The sensible conclusion is neither to abandon flagship species nor to treat them as a complete strategy. They are a tool for raising attention and money, and a useful one. But a conservation movement that allowed the tastes of donors to draw its map of priorities would leave large gaps, and those gaps would fall precisely where the most unfamiliar forms of life are found. Some part of the effort has to be directed by need rather than by appeal, even when need comes in the shape of a mussel.
R06-B-03: When a population of elephants recovers, the news is usually reported as a conservation triumph, and in an important sense it is one. But the recovery is experienced very differently at the edge of the forest. For a farming household whose maize or paddy lies along an elephant's route, a single night's visit can destroy a season's income, and the danger is not only to crops: people walking home after dark, or guarding fields from makeshift platforms, are injured and sometimes killed. The benefits of a thriving elephant population are spread thinly across a nation, or across the world; its costs are concentrated on a few villages. Discussions of the problem often frame it as one of attitudes. Farmers who retaliate, it is said, need to be taught to value wildlife, and coexistence is presented as a disposition that can be cultivated through awareness campaigns. There is something to this, since tolerance of wild animals varies a great deal between communities and is shaped by tradition as well as by loss. Yet to treat hostility as ignorance is to misread it. A farmer who has lost three harvests to elephants may understand their ecological importance perfectly well and still be unable to afford them. The more honest framing is distributive. Coexistence is not a state of mind but an arrangement about who bears which costs. Compensation schemes acknowledge this in principle, but in practice they are often slow, demand paperwork that poor households struggle to complete, and pay for the market value of a damaged crop while ignoring the sleepless nights, the children kept from school to guard fields and the fear that hangs over every harvest. A scheme that pays a fraction of the loss, a year late, does not shift the burden; it documents it. Practical deterrents have their place. Some communities have experimented with fences hung with beehives, which elephants tend to avoid, or with repellents made from chilli and with networks that warn villages of approaching herds, and where these work they reduce losses at modest cost. But deterrents move the problem as often as they solve it, pushing elephants onto the next village's fields. The underlying question remains political: whether the wider society that values elephants is willing to pay, promptly and in full, those who live beside them. Until it is, appeals for tolerance ask the poorest people in the landscape to subsidise everyone else's enjoyment of a recovered species.
R06-B-04: For much of the twentieth century, forest agencies in several countries treated fire as an enemy to be defeated wherever it appeared. The logic seemed unanswerable: fire destroys timber, threatens homes and kills animals, so every fire extinguished was a loss averted. Agencies measured their performance by how quickly they put fires out and how few hectares burned, and by those measures many of them succeeded remarkably well. Lookout towers, firebreaks and crews ready to move at short notice made it possible to reach most fires while they were still small. The success contained its own reversal. In many dry forests, frequent fires of low intensity had once cleared the undergrowth, fallen branches and young trees that gather on the forest floor, while leaving the older, thick-barked trees largely unharmed. When such fires were suppressed year after year, that material was left to build up. The forest grew denser, and the fuel that would once have burned off in small, manageable fires accumulated until, in a hot, dry season, a fire that could not be stopped found enough of it to climb into the crowns of the trees. Such fires kill the very trees that the earlier, smaller ones had spared. By preventing many small fires, suppression had, in effect, been saving up for a few enormous ones. The lesson is sometimes drawn too broadly. Not every ecosystem evolved with frequent fire; in some wet forests and many shrublands fire was historically rare, and a recent increase in burning there is a threat rather than a return to normal. Nor does the history of suppression explain every catastrophic fire, since drought, heat and the spread of housing into wooded land matter as well. The argument is not that fire is good, but that whether a given fire is harmful depends on the ecosystem in which it burns and on that ecosystem's history. Recognising this has not made the remedy easy. Deliberately setting fires under controlled conditions, or allowing some natural fires to burn, can reduce accumulated fuel, but it carries risks that suppression appeared not to. Politically, a season without burning looks like competence. Smoke drifts over towns, and a planned burn that escapes is blamed on the people who lit it, while a wildfire that grows from decades of accumulated fuel is blamed on nature. A manager therefore faces an asymmetry. The harm of acting is visible and attributable; the harm of not acting is deferred and diffuse, and the easiest course is to keep doing what made the problem worse.
R06-B-05: The model of the national park that spread across much of the world in the twentieth century rested on a simple picture: nature is most fully itself where people are absent, and the task of conservation is to keep them out. Boundaries were drawn, guards were posted, and in many places the people who had lived within the new boundaries, herding, gathering, farming small plots or hunting, were moved elsewhere. Critics have come to call this approach fortress conservation, and the name captures both its method and its mood. The picture of untouched nature was often historically false. Many landscapes that visitors admired as wilderness had been shaped for centuries by the people who were then removed: grasslands kept open by grazing and deliberate burning, forests whose composition reflected generations of selective harvesting and planting. Removing those people did not return the land to an original state; it began a new and unplanned experiment, and in some cases the very qualities that had made the place worth protecting began to decline. The costs to the displaced were, of course, more direct: the loss of homes, of access to food and medicine, of graves and sacred places, often with little or no compensation. It would be too simple, however, to conclude that local residents are always the best stewards and that exclusion is never justified. Communities change, markets reach into forests, and a population that once harvested lightly may, under new pressures, begin to clear or hunt at rates the land cannot sustain. Some species, particularly those that are very sensitive to disturbance, may genuinely need areas where human presence is kept to a minimum. The romantic image of the timeless forest dweller can be as misleading as the image of untouched wilderness that it seeks to replace. What the critique of fortress conservation establishes, then, is not a rule but a burden of proof. Exclusion imposes certain and heavy costs on identifiable people, while its benefits to wildlife are often assumed rather than shown. Where those who would be displaced have a long record of use compatible with the values being protected, the presumption should lie with their remaining, and with arrangements that give them a real share in managing the land. Where that record is absent, or where a species' needs are demonstrably incompatible with human use, exclusion may be defended; but it must be defended, case by case, rather than taken as the natural form of protection.
R06-B-06: The idea of a keystone species borrows its name from architecture. In an arch, the keystone is the wedge at the top that holds the other stones in place; remove it, and the structure falls. Applied to ecosystems, the term picks out species whose effect on their community is far larger than their abundance would suggest, so that their loss sets off changes that ripple through many other species. A predator that keeps a grazer in check, allowing plants to flourish, is the classic case, and the concept has proved enormously useful in persuading the public and governments that the fate of a single species can matter to a whole landscape. The vividness of the metaphor, however, carries assumptions that ecology does not always support. An arch has one keystone, and its role is fixed by the geometry of the structure. Ecological communities are not like this. The same species may have a dominant influence in one place and a minor one in another, depending on what else lives there, on the climate and on the history of the site. A predator that controls its prey on a rocky shore where that prey has few other enemies may matter much less where the prey is also eaten by several other animals. Keystone status, in other words, is a property of a relationship in a particular setting, not a fixed attribute of a species. The metaphor also invites a search for the one species that holds everything together, when in many communities influence is spread across several species, each of moderate importance, whose combined effects are what keep the system stable. A conservation strategy built around identifying and protecting keystones may then direct attention to a few dramatic interactions and neglect the diffuse ones, which are harder to demonstrate but not necessarily less important. The absence of a striking keystone in a community does not show that its members are interchangeable. None of this means the concept should be discarded. Some species really do have outsized and well-documented effects, and naming them helps in arguing for their protection. The danger lies in treating the label as a discovery about a species' nature rather than a finding about a particular system, and in assuming that where no keystone has been identified, no species is indispensable. The architectural image is best used as what it is, a way of making one kind of ecological fact memorable, and not as a model of how communities are generally built.
R06-B-07: Conservationists have long sorted species into two kinds. Native species belong where they are found and deserve protection; alien species, carried by people beyond their former range, are suspect, and those that spread are labelled invasive and targeted for control. The distinction is so familiar that it is rarely examined, yet it rests on a choice that is not itself ecological. To call a species native is to say that it was present before some date, usually the arrival of a particular wave of human travel or trade, and the date is a convention. Species have always moved, carried by winds, currents and birds or on their own legs, and as the climate warms many are shifting their ranges without any human hand to carry them. A plant that crosses a mountain range by itself is not usually called an invader; one that crosses in a shipment of grain is. A growing number of ecologists conclude that origin should simply be dropped as a criterion. What matters, they argue, is what a species does. Many introduced species cause no measurable harm, and some are positively useful: they hold soil on eroded slopes, feed pollinators where native flowers have been lost, or provide cover for native birds in landscapes that offer little else. Campaigns to remove such species spend scarce money and can do damage of their own, through herbicides, through disturbance of the ground, or by stripping out shelter on which native animals had come to depend. Judging species by their passports rather than by their effects is, on this view, a kind of ecological nativism, and conservation would do better without it. The critics are right that origin is not itself a harm, and right that much eradication has been undertaken without asking whether the target was doing any damage. But their alternative assumes that effects can be known at the moment a decision has to be made, and this is often false. Introduced species frequently remain scarce and inconspicuous for decades before something, a change in climate, a new road, the arrival of a suitable pollinator, allows them to spread rapidly. By the time the harm is plain, removal has usually become impossible. Moreover, a newly arrived species has no shared history with the predators, parasites and competitors of its new home, and so its future behaviour there is harder to forecast than that of a species whose relationships have been worked out over a long time. This does not make the newcomer more likely to be harmful; it makes its effects less predictable, which is a different thing. Seen this way, origin is neither a verdict nor an irrelevance but a piece of evidence, and what it is evidence of is uncertainty. Its weight changes with time. When a species has only just arrived, removal is cheap and its effects are unknown, and a presumption against it is reasonable precisely because the decision cannot wait for the evidence that the critics demand. When a species has been established for a century and its effects can be observed, the presumption has done its work, and the case for removing it should rest on what it is shown to do; the label alien then adds little. Both the defenders of the old distinction and its critics treat the question as one of identity, of what a species is. It is better understood as a question of timing and of knowledge: of what can be known about a species, and when.
R06-B-08: Ecological restoration has traditionally worked towards a picture. A degraded marsh or heath is compared with a reference state, usually the condition of the site at some earlier date as reconstructed from records, maps or surviving fragments, and success is measured by how closely the site comes to resemble it. Rewilding, in many of its versions, refuses this. Rather than aiming at a particular assemblage of species, it seeks to restore processes: grazing and browsing by large herbivores, the flooding of rivers that have been confined to channels, predation, the falling and rotting of trees. What the landscape then becomes is left open. Its advocates present this refusal to name an end state not as a gap in the method but as its central virtue. Their reasons are serious. Any reference state is chosen, not found: a site has passed through many conditions, and to select one of them as the true or original form of the place is to privilege one moment of its history over all the others. Under a changing climate, moreover, the conditions that sustained a historical community may no longer exist, so that holding a landscape to an old picture would require ever more intervention, mowing, planting, culling and weeding on a scale that amounts to gardening, however large the garden. Better, the argument runs, to set processes going and accept whatever community they produce. The obvious objection is that a project with no target cannot fail. If whatever emerges is by definition what nature has chosen, then no outcome, however disappointing, counts as evidence against the project, and those who fund it, live beside it or simply care about the place are left with no way to hold it to account. The objection becomes sharper when the results are unwelcome: when scrub swallows a flower-rich meadow that people valued, or when a rare species that depended on the old management quietly disappears. To answer that this, too, is nature taking its course is to make the project immune to criticism, and a claim that nothing could count against is not much of a claim. Advocates have a partial reply. A project can be held to account for its processes even if not for its outcome: one can ask whether the river is in fact allowed to flood, whether herbivore numbers rise and fall with the food available rather than being fixed by managers, whether dead wood is left where it falls. These are checkable commitments, and a project that fails to keep them has failed in a sense that matters. But the reply does not dissolve the difficulty, because the choice of processes is itself a choice about outcomes. Which animals are released, in what numbers, within what fences and over how large an area will go a long way towards deciding whether the land becomes closed woodland, open pasture or something between, and often these consequences can be foreseen. A few cattle and ponies at low density on a large area will produce a different landscape from many of them on a small one, and those who set the density know this. What rewilding achieves, then, is not the withdrawal of human choice from the landscape but its relocation, from the end of the process to its beginning. This is not an argument against rewilding, which may well be the most sensible response available in a world where no historical picture can be held still. It is an argument against a certain way of describing it. The phrase 'letting nature decide' conceals decisions that people have already made, and the method is more honest, and more open to the scrutiny it needs, when its advocates own those decisions.
